Q A2 
What is the syntax and use of the relative addressing mode? 
Syntax: 
Effective Address (EA) = PC + Offset 
Use: 
In relative addressing mode, the operand address is obtained by adding a signed offset to the current 
Program Counter (PC). It is commonly used for branch and jump instructions  to support 
position-independent code. [2]

What is the key advantage of associative mapping over direct mapping? 
The key advantage of associative mapping is that any block of main memory can be placed in 
any cache line , which significantly reduces cache conflicts and miss rate  compared to direct 
mapping. [2]

Q B1 A program consists of four instruction types A, B, C, and D. Instruction A has a CPI of 1.3 and 
accounts for 60% of the instructions. Instruction B has a CPI of 2.2 and occurs 10% of the time. [6]
 CO1 

Instruction C has a CPI of 2.0 with a frequency of 20%, and instruction D has a CPI of 2.8 with a 
frequency of 10%. The CPU designer proposes two options:
   (a) reduce the CPI of instruction A to 
1.1, or
   (b) reduce the CPI of instructions B and D to 1.6. Which option gives better performance? 
A program has four instruction types A, B, C and D with the following CPI and instruction mix: 
Instruction A: CPI = 1.3, Frequency = 60% 
Instruction B: CPI = 2.2, Frequency = 10% 
Instruction C: CPI = 2.0, Frequency = 20% 
Instruction D: CPI = 2.8, Frequency = 10% 
Average CPI before improvement: 
Average CPI 
= (1.3 × 0.6) + (2.2 × 0.1) + (2.0 × 0.2) + (2.8 × 0.1) 
= 0.78 + 0.22 + 0.40 + 0.28 
= 1.68 
 
Option
   (a): Reduce CPI of instruction A to 1.1 
New Average CPI 
= (1.1 × 0.6) + (2.2 × 0.1) + (2.0 × 0.2) + (2.8 × 0.1) 
= 0.66 + 0.22 + 0.40 + 0.28 
= 1.56 
 
Option
   (b): Reduce CPI of instructions B and D to 1.6 
New Average CPI 
= (1.3 × 0.6) + (1.6 × 0.1) + (2.0 × 0.2) + (1.6 × 0.1) 
= 0.78 + 0.16 + 0.40 + 0.16 
= 1.50 
 
Conclusion: 
Since the average CPI is lower in Option
   (b), reducing the CPI of instructions B and D gives 
better performance.

Q B2 
Illustrate architecture of a vector processor with its advantages. 
A vector processor is designed to perform operations on one-dimensional arrays (vectors) of 
data using a single instruction. 
Main Components: 
1. Vector Register File (VRF) 
o Contains a set of vector registers. 
o Each vector register holds multiple data elements. 
2. Vector Functional Units 
o Dedicated arithmetic units for vector operations such as: 
▪ Vector add 
▪ Vector multiply 
▪ Vector divide [6]
 CO1 
▪ Vector compare 
3. Vector Control Unit 
o Decodes vector instructions. 
o Generates control signals for vector operations. 
4. Scalar Processor 
o Executes scalar instructions. 
o Handles loop control, branching, and address calculations. 
5. Memory System 
o Supports high-bandwidth memory access. 
o Allows vector load and store operations.

Advantages of Vector Processors 
1. High performance for scientific and numerical applications 
2. Reduced instruction fetch and decode overhead 
3. Better utilization of pipelined hardware 
4. Efficient handling of loops and array operations 
5. Simpler control compared to superscalar processors 
6. High throughput due to parallel element processing

Q B3 
Suppose multiple devices capable of generating interrupts are connected to a CPU. Describe two 
possible methods the CPU can use to identify the interrupting device and obtain the starting address 
of the corresponding Interrupt Service Routine (ISR). 
1. Vectored Interrupts
   • The interrupting device supplies an interrupt vector number.
   • CPU uses this vector to directly obtain ISR address from a table. [6]
 CO3
   • Fast and efficient, commonly used in modern systems. 
 
2. Polling (Non-vectored Interrupts)
   • CPU checks devices one by one to identify the interrupt source.
   • ISR starting address is obtained after identifying the device.
   • Simple but slow method.

Q B4 
Consider a 4-way set associative cache of size 32 KB with a block size of 128 bytes. If the main 
memory size is 512 KB, determine number of bits in the tag and size of the tag directory. 
Given: 
Cache size = 32 KB 
Block size = 128 bytes 
Cache type = 4-way set associative 
Main memory size = 512 KB

   Step 1: Number of cache blocks 
Cache size = 32 KB = 32 × 1024 = 32768 bytes 
Number of blocks 
= 32768 / 128 
= 256 blocks

   Step 2: Number of sets 
4-way set associative cache 
Number of sets 
= 256 / 4 
= 64 sets 
Index bits 
= log₂64 
= 6 bits

   Step 3: Block offset bits 
Block size = 128 bytes 
Offset bits 
= log₂128 
= 7 bits

   Step 4: Main memory address bits 
Main memory size = 512 KB 
= 512 × 1024 bytes 
= 2¹⁹ bytes 
Main memory address bits 
= 19 bits [6]
 CO3

   Step 5: Tag bits 
Tag bits 
= Total address bits − (Index bits + Offset bits) 
= 19 − (6 + 7) 
= 6 bits

   Step 6: Size of tag directory 
Total cache lines = 256 
Tag directory size 
= 256 × 6 
= 1536 bits 
 
Final Answer: 
Number of tag bits = 6 bits 
Size of tag directory = 1536 bits

Q C1 
Consider a byte-addressable machine with a 32-bit word size. An array of n 32-bit integers is stored 
in consecutive memory locations starting at address ARR, and the value of n is stored as a 32 -bit 
integer at memory location N. Write an assembly language program to find the maximum element 
of the array and store the result in memory location MAX, without using any additional array or 
temporary storage other than registers.
   LOAD    R1, N          ; R1 ← n (number of elements)
   LOAD    R2, ARR        ; R2 ← first array element (max = ARR[0])
   ADD     R3, ARR, #4    ; R3 ← address of next element (ARR + 4) 
 
LOOP:
   SUB     R1, R1, #1     ; decrement count
   BEQ     DONE           ; if all elements checked, exit loop
   LOAD    R0, 0(R3)      ; R0 ← current array element
   CMP     R0, R2         ; compare current element with max
   BLE     SKIP           ; if R0 ≤ R2, skip update
   MOVE    R2, R0         ; update max value 
 
SKIP:
   ADD     R3, R3, #4     ; move to next array element
   BR      LOOP           ; repeat loop 
 
DONE:
   STORE   R2, MAX        ; store maximum value in MAX
   HALT
   Explanation (for answer writing)
   • Register R2 holds the current maximum value.
   • Register R3 points to the next array element.
   • Register R1 stores the remaining number of elements.
   • The program scans the array once, compares each element with the current maximum, and 
updates it if required.
   • No additional memory locations or arrays are used. [10]
 CO2
